name: Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres

src.name: Wikipedia · Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres
src.q: In March 1797, the Academy awarded Ingres first prize in drawing, and in August he traveled to Paris to study in the studio of Jacques-Louis David, France's—and Europe's—leading painter during the revolutionary period, in whose studio he remained for four years.

notes.name: Wikipedia · Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres
notes.q: Ingres painted a new portrait of Napoleon for presentation at the Salon of 1806, this one showing Napoleon on the Imperial Throne for his coronation.

notes.name: Wikipedia · Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres
notes.q: On 23 November 1806, he wrote to Jean Forestier, the father of his former fiancée, "Yes, art will need to be reformed, and I intend to be that revolutionary."

notes.name: Wikipedia · Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres
notes.q: Ingres wrote with enthusiasm that he had been planning to paint this subject since 1806, and he intended to "deploy all of the luxury of art in its beauty".

src.name: Wikipedia · Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres
src.q: While working in Rome and subsequently Florence from 1806 to 1824, he regularly sent paintings to the Paris Salon, where they were faulted by critics who found his style bizarre and archaic.

notes.name: Wikipedia · Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres
notes.q: Ingres continued to suffer disparaging reviews, as Don Pedro of Toledo Kissing Henry IV's Sword, Raphael and the Fornarina (Fogg Art Museum, Harvard University), several portraits, and the Interior of the Sistine Chapel met with generally hostile critical response at the Paris Salon of 1814.

src.name: Wikipedia · Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres
src.q: He traveled to Naples in the spring of 1814 to paint Queen Caroline Murat.

notes.name: Wikipedia · Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres
notes.q: In 1815 he painted Aretino and Charles V's Ambassador as well as Aretino and Tintoretto, an anecdotal painting whose subject, a painter brandishing a pistol at his critic, may have been especially satisfying to the embattled Ingres.

notes.name: Wikipedia · Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres
notes.q: In 1819 he sent his reclining nude, La Grande Odalisque, as well as a history painting, Philip V and the Marshal of Berwick, and Roger Freeing Angelica, based on an episode in the 16th-century epic poem Orlando Furioso by Ariosto but his work was once again condemned by critics as gothic and unnatural.

notes.q: Completed in 1820, this imposing work was well received in Rome but to the artist's chagrin the ecclesiastical authorities there would not permit it to be sent to Paris for exhibition.

src.name: Wikipedia · Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres
src.q: In 1820 Ingres and his wife moved to Florence at the urging of the Florentine sculptor Lorenzo Bartolini, an old friend from his years in Paris.

notes.name: Wikipedia · Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres
notes.q: He was finally recognized at the Salon in 1824, when his Raphaelesque painting, The Vow of Louis XIII, was met with acclaim, and Ingres was acknowledged as the leader of the Neoclassical school in France.

notes.name: Wikipedia · Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres
notes.q: He spent four years bringing the large canvas to completion, and he took it to the Paris Salon in October 1824, where it became the key that finally opened the door of the Paris art establishment and to his career as an official painter.

notes.name: Wikipedia · Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres
notes.q: The Vow of Louis XIII in the Salon of 1824 finally brought Ingres critical success.

src.q: He traveled to Orvieto (1835), Siena (1835), and to Ravenna and Urbino to study the paleochristian mosaics, medieval murals and Renaissance art.
